newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Political instability curbs tourism in Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Political instability curbs tourism in Serbia.

text.p: Serbia's tourist industry faces another wasted year in 1997 due to political instability and tourism earnings will not reach the target of 100 million marks ($60 million), industry sources said on Tuesday.
Hotel operators and caterers have appealed to both the government and opposition parties to create a stable environment.

"The whole economy has come to a standstill. Companies are not working and hotels are empty. The blockade is more drastic than U.N. sanctions," said Ratko Uljarevic, chairman of the department for toursim and catering in the Chamber of Commerce.
"Even if street protests stop tomorrow, we will need at least three months to recover," Uljarevic said.

"Tourism cannot function when the rest of the economy has run aground. What can you offer to tourists when you cannot grant them elementary security," Njegomir Kilibarda, who runs the Mladost Hotel, said.
According to a report by the department for tourism, the number of tourists halved in January from December because of political instability.
A plunge in the standard of living of Yugoslavs and a decline in the number of visitors from abroad have hit the industry.
Many foreigners, mainly from Greece, Hungary, Russia and Israel, cancelled plans for New Year and Christmas holidays in Serbian ski resorts due to the political crisis, the report said.
It gave no comparative figures. Final 1996 results are due in early March. According to official statistics, the Yugoslav tourism industry earned around $40.2 million from January to November 1996.
The industry is also suffering from high fiscal burdens, insolvency and the closure of banks.

The director of the Bukovicka Banja spa hotels, Zdravko Dukic, said the state had to make clear which banks would survive. Serbian hotels and restaurants, which suffered from 3-1/2 years of international trade embargo, need money to upgrade.
The tourism industry also wants the government to abolish visas for foreigners and reduce high road tolls for foreign vehicles.

Apart from two million dinars promised by the government to step up Serbia's tourism campaign abroad, hotel operators have called on the state to design a long-term development strategy for the industry. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254 ($ = 1.666 German Marks)
